Check Point Launches Firewall-as-a-Subscription as Cybersecurity Budgets Face Growing Pressure
items.summary: Check Point Software Technologies has announced the launch of Firewall-as-a-Subscription, a new offering designed to make advanced AI-powered network security more accessible to organisations without requiring a significant upfront hardware investment. The new subscription model gives businesses access to Check Point Force Firewalls, AI-powered threat prevention and agentic security management through predictable monthly or annual payments. The offering is designed to help organisations modernise their network defences while managing increasingly constrained cybersecurity budgets. The announcement comes as businesses face growing financial pressures, with inflation and higher borrowing costs forcing many to delay infrastructure upgrades. According to the IANS Research and Artico Search 2026 Security Budget Benchmark , the median cybersecurity budget remained unchanged this year, with 55% of CISOs reporting flat or declining budgets. Although 64% requested additional funding, just 45% received an increase. These financial constraints are emerging at a time when AI adoption is introducing new challenges for network security, including the need to inspect AI-generated traffic, protect AI applications and monitor autonomous agents. Check Point’s Firewall-as-a-Subscription aims to address these challenges by removing the need for large capital investments, allowing organisations to access advanced security capabilities through a subscription-based model. The offering builds on Check Point’s R82.20 release, introduced in July 2026, which brought AI Network Firewall capabilities designed to inspect AI traffic, protect AI applications and help govern AI agents at the network layer. The subscription includes Check Point Force Firewalls, with capacity and pricing based on the threat prevention throughput required by each organisation. Customers also receive AI-powered threat prevention, including SandBlast technology, which Check Point claims achieves a 99.9% block rate against zero-day attacks. Additional features include Live Updates, which enable security updates without reboots or downtime, and Smart-1 cloud-based agentic management. The package also includes 24/7 premium support and professional services credits to assist with activities such as migrating firewall policies from other vendors. Under the three-year subscription, organisations can increase their firewall throughput as their requirements evolve, with the option to move to new hardware after 36 months. Pete Finalle, Research Manager, Security and Trust at IDC, commented on the growing demand for more flexible security purchasing models. “Organizations of all sizes face the same AI-driven threats, but for many, capital budget cycles often force them to delay firewall refreshes or buy more capacity than they need,” he said. “Consumption models that turn on-premises security hardware into a predictable operating expense, and let organizations scale protection as their needs grow, can help close that gap. We expect demand for this kind of flexibility to rise as AI adoption increases the traffic and risk networks must handle.” The subscription model could also provide opportunities for channel partners to help customers progress firewall refresh projects that have been delayed by capital expenditure restrictions. Avi Rembaum, President Global Technical Sales at Check Point Software Technologies, said: “Every organization is adopting AI, and every organization deserves the same level of protection, whatever its size or budget. “With Firewall-as-a-Subscription, we are making our most advanced AI security, threat prevention and agentic management available through one simple subscription, so organizations can secure their AI transformation today.” Check Point Firewall-as-a-Subscription will be available from 1 November 2026 through Check Point’s partner network, with monthly and annual payment options.

items.title: Popcorn Time’s forgotten updater left millions of devices exposed to hijacking
items.summary: You may have forgotten about Popcorn Time. Unfortunately, its updater didn’t forget about your device. Security researchers have intervened to disable an abandoned update mechanism in Time4Popcorn, a version of the once-popular streaming app. If left running in the background, the updater could have allowed attackers to take control of Windows and Mac computers, even if their owners hadn’t opened the app in years. Eye Security estimates that the vulnerable updater was present on millions of devices worldwide, including 2.5–3 million Windows computers and around 250,000–350,000 Macs. Popcorn Time made watching movies and TV shows through BitTorrent look more like browsing Netflix. Rather than making users find torrent files and open them in a separate client, it wrapped the process in a familiar streaming-style interface. Amid concerns about copyright infringement and its possible consequences, the original developers abandoned it shortly after its launch in 2014. But because its source code was publicly available, other developers could pick it up and create their own versions, known as forks. One of those was Time4Popcorn, which was also distributed under the name “Popcorn Time.” That shared branding matters because people may have installed the affected software without ever seeing the Time4Popcorn name. The problem at hand Time4Popcorn was eventually abandoned too. But its update infrastructure was left behind, and at some point the domains associated with the software became available for others to register. In other words, the people maintaining the software had gone away. The software’s ability to accept instructions had not. Time4Popcorn’s updater used unencrypted HTTP connections and accepted executable updates without checking digital signatures to verify their authenticity. So, someone who controlled an update domain or was able to tamper with the unencrypted traffic could supply their own program instead. That combination created a remote code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-30612 , which could let an attacker run malicious software on a device. An attacker wouldn’t need to persuade someone to watch a movie or click a suspicious attachment. The forgotten updater could do the work for them. Although Android was affected too, users had an extra layer of protection. Its updater checked for updates when the application was opened, but installing an attacker-supplied APK required the user to approve the installation. It was not the same silent, background takeover route researchers found on Windows and macOS. What the researchers did Eye Security registered an abandoned update domain and used the vulnerable mechanism to distribute an update that disabled the updater itself. On Windows, it stopped and disabled the service; on macOS, it prevented the update process from starting. The researchers say their intervention did not delete users’ files or collect host data. By March 2026, Eye Security reported more than two million downloads of its updater-disabling fix, and update requests to its domains had fallen by 98%. Later that month, it transferred the 15 domains it controlled to the nonprofit Shadowserver Foundation . Researchers could not remotely disable the Android updater in the same way. And the desktop application still contained other weaknesses, including an obsolete Chrome engine dating from 2014 and disabled sandbox protections, which normally help contain malicious code. What users should do If you used Popcorn Time years ago, check the devices on which you installed it. Don’t assume that no longer using an application means its background components have stopped running. Check your list of installed applications for Popcorn Time or Time4Popcorn. Pay particular attention to older Windows PCs, Macs, and Android devices where you may have forgotten about installing it. The affected fork was distributed under both names. Remove the old application. There is no vendor security update for the abandoned Time4Popcorn software. Disabling the updater addresses one vulnerability, not the application’s other security weaknesses. On Windows and macOS, check that the background updater is no longer running. Eye Security identifies the Windows component as Updater.exe , normally inside a Popcorn Time folder under Program Files or Program Files (x86), running through a service called Update Service. On macOS, the component is /Library/PrivilegedHelperTools/PT.updd , with a launch daemon at /Library/LaunchDaemons/PT.updd.plist . Its advisory provides instructions for disabling these components if needed. On Android, uninstall the affected app rather than accepting an update prompt from it. The updater is part of the main application and cannot easily be disabled separately. Use an up-to-date, real-time anti-malware solution to detect and block any attempts to install malware on your devices. As we saw recently , cybercriminals can use software updates to distribute malware. Remove abandoned apps and check for any background updaters they leave behind. items.title: Introducing the Magnet AI Research Lab: Our first peer-reviewed study puts AI in digital forensics to the test
items.summary: By Brandon Epstein Key takeaways: Magnet Forensics has launched the Magnet AI Research Lab, a dedicated program for applied AI research in digital forensics. The Research Lab’s first study , published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences, tested how accurately trained examiners and an AI expert system interpret media authentication results. The expert system scored 22 percentage points higher than the human average. Every digital forensic examiner has been asked some version of the same question on the stand: how do you know? It’s a fair question, and for most of the tools we use every day the answer depends on research somebody conducted and published. That isn’t a unique expectation. It applies to every forensic science, from firearms to toxicology, and just as squarely to the use of AI in digital forensics . Today Magnet Forensics is launching the Magnet AI Research Lab : a dedicated program for research into the use of AI in digital forensics. The Lab exists because that question is getting harder to answer. Courts have been weighing the reliability of novel science since before Daubert , and the questions haven’t gone away. The 2009 National Academy of Sciences report Strengthening Forensic Science in the United States found that, apart from nuclear DNA analysis, no forensic method had been rigorously shown to reliably connect evidence to a specific individual or source. The President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology (PCAST) reached a similar conclusion in 2016 . The traditional disciplines named in those reports responded by doing the work. Digital forensics is moving in the right direction, but the road ahead is long, and the technology moves considerably faster. AI didn’t create that gap. It turned the volume up on it. Holding ourselves to the standard we are asking for A good blog post or whitepaper can be genuinely informative and useful. It can explain a method clearly, share data, and help practitioners understand what a tool does and why. We publish plenty of them . Proving that technology works is a different job. That’s why the Magnet AI Research Lab not only conducts research, but submits its studies to peer-reviewed journals, where independent reviewers decide whether the methodology holds. If the results don’t survive that process, they don’t get published. Once they are published, anyone can find the paper and review the study themselves. What the Magnet AI Research Lab does The Magnet AI Research Lab conducts and publishes its own research: studies on AI in digital forensics, which are submitted to peer-reviewed journals and conference proceedings so practitioners and courts can have confidence in the efficacy of results rather than take our word for it. The Lab also partners on research with both practitioners and academics. A lot of excellent academic work never reaches the bench, not because it’s poor quality, but because it answers a different question than the one the examiner needed answered or never consults an examiner at all. Meanwhile, examiners face the questions that matter most without the methodology, statistical support, or the time to answer them. The Lab is designed to close that gap: helping with the research, the writing, and the publishing, or connecting an examiner to an academic partner who can. The Lab is also a conduit. This is the part we most want people to hear. If you have a research question and genuinely don’t know where to start, you don’t need a methodology first. Come as you are, with the artifact that has been bothering you for years, and we’ll help you work out what the question actually is and who is best placed to answer it. The Lab’s first study shows what that looks like in practice. Can AI interpret media authentication better than a human examiner? The study, published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences , is Evaluating the use of a novel expert system for interpretation of media authentication results , by Brandon Epstein, Bertram Lyons, Daniel Fischer, and Albert Zlogar. It asked a deliberately narrow question. Media authentication answers questions like whether a photo or video is a genuine original, is an edited file, or synthetic media generated by AI — the deep end of the forensics pool, where the signals have to be read together before an examiner can say what a file really is. So, we built a test to find out who reads those signals more accurately: a trained human examiner, or the AI expert system inside Magnet Verify . Magnet Verify’s Automated Analysis, which is powered by AI, is used to confirm the authenticity of digital evidence through the analysis of hundreds of signals generated within Magnet Verify. Here’s how it worked: 14 video files were created for the study, consisting of camera originals, edited files, social media files, AI-generated media, and a few designed specifically not to match anything in the Magnet Verify reference library. We stripped out any automated analysis and Magnet Verify branding from the results, then asked trained, experienced examiners to provide an opinion about each file’s authenticity. We then ran the same files through Magnet Verify’s automated analysis expert system and scored both the human and machine-generated responses against the ground truth data of the sample output. The result Across 20 respondents, the human mean was 69%. The expert system scored 91% — outperforming the human average by 22 percentage points. Just as important as the score: the system didn’t return a single incorrect answer. Where the data didn’t support a confident call, it said so rather than guessing, which is exactly the behavior you want from a tool whose output might end up in front of a court. The human results were revealing on their own. What predicted a high score wasn’t years on the job, it was specialized media authentication training . Experience alone showed no correlation at all. That says something about how hard this skill is to build and how thinly it’s spread across the field, which is a key reason a system that performs consistently matters. How the headline result is framed matters, too. This isn’t a story about the machine being smarter than the examiner. These were layered, complicated results, and the expert system has a few unglamorous advantages: it doesn’t get tired, it doesn’t skip steps, and it is not biased by irrelevant case data. This isn’t replacing the examiner — it’s providing another tool to help produce accurate results. Have a research question, dataset, or potential study in mind? Connect with the Lab to start a conversation. Learn more about the Magnet AI Research Lab . About the author Brandon Epstein is Principal Digital Forensics Specialist at Magnet Forensics, where he leads the Magnet AI Research Lab. A former police detective and co-founder of Medex Forensics, which Magnet acquired in 2024, Brandon specializes in AI and media authentication and is active in many digital forensic community organizations.

items.title: The SonarQube Remediation Agent now fixes Hunter Agent findings
items.summary: In August, SonarQube Hunter Agent became generally available on SonarQube Cloud, giving teams a way to find the security flaws that pattern-based analysis misses. Broken access control, business logic flaws, and gaps in authentication and session handling now show up as SonarQube issues, and each one is checked before it is raised. Finding them was half the job. Each finding still waited for someone to write the fix. The SonarQube Remediation Agent now takes on that second half. On SonarQube Cloud, you can send Hunter Agent findings from your main branch to the agent and get each fix back as a pull request. Hunter Agent finds the flaw. The Remediation Agent proposes the change. Your team decides what merges. Why are logic flaws harder to fix than other issues? A logic flaw is not a broken line of code. The code runs exactly as written. The problem is what it lets someone do. Take a classic case. An endpoint returns an invoice by its ID and never checks that the invoice belongs to the caller’s organization. Any signed-in user can read another customer’s invoice by changing a number in the URL. There is no injection and no unsafe call. Nothing in the code matches a known bad pattern. The fix is rarely long, but it is hard to get right. You need to know how your application identifies the caller, where ownership lives in your data model, and how the rest of the codebase already enforces it. Get that wrong and you either leave the hole open or break a legitimate workflow. So these findings often wait for whoever knows the access model best. How does the Remediation Agent fix a Hunter Agent finding? It starts from a finding that has already been checked. Hunter Agent tests each candidate to rule out false positives. It then raises the finding as a vulnerability with a severity, an exact location in the code, and an explanation in two parts: why it is an issue, and how to fix it. The Remediation Agent works from that finding and from your full repository, not just the lines that were flagged. The workflow is the one your team may already use for backlog fixes: Open your project’s Issues page and select the main branch. Turn on the Fixable by Agent filter. Eligible Hunter Agent findings appear alongside your other fixable issues. To see only Hunter Agent findings, add the hunter-agent tag, or a category tag such as hunter-broken-access-control . Select the findings you want fixed, up to 20 at a time, and choose Fix with Agent . Follow the run on the Remediation Agent page. When a fix is available, open the linked pull request, review it, and merge it. The agent generates each change through your organization’s own OpenAI or Anthropic key, and verifies the proposed change before it opens a pull request. Why does each finding get its own pull request? For rule-based issues, the agent groups the fixes you assign by rule key and file type. Hunter Agent findings are handled differently. Each finding gets its own pull request, or merge request on Github, when a fix is available. That fits security work. One pull request maps to one finding. As with other backlog fixes from the agent, the pull request summary describes the issue it addresses in the same format you see in SonarQube. A reviewer can judge an access control change on its own, without untangling it from five others. If one fix needs a longer conversation, it does not hold the rest back. What does a fix for a logic flaw look like? Here is the invoice example from earlier, simplified: @GetMapping("/invoices/{id}") public Invoice get(@PathVariable Long id) { // Returns any invoice by ID. Nothing checks the caller's tenant. return invoiceRepo.findById(id).orElseThrow(); } Hunter Agent flags this kind of code as an authorization bypass through a user-controlled key (CWE-639). A good fix scopes the lookup to the caller, so the endpoint can only return invoices the caller is allowed to see. In August, SonarQube Hunter Agent became generally available on SonarQube Cloud, giving teams a way to find the security flaws that pattern-based analysis misses. Broken access control, business logic flaws, and gaps in authentication and session handling now show up as SonarQube issues, and each one is checked before it is raised.

Finding them was half the job. Each finding still waited for someone to write the fix.

The SonarQube Remediation Agent now takes on that second half. On SonarQube Cloud, you can send Hunter Agent findings from your main branch to the agent and get each fix back as a pull request. Hunter Agent finds the flaw. The Remediation Agent proposes the change. Your team decides what merges.

Why are logic flaws harder to fix than other issues?

A logic flaw is not a broken line of code. The code runs exactly as written. The problem is what it lets someone do.

Take a classic case. An endpoint returns an invoice by its ID and never checks that the invoice belongs to the caller’s organization. Any signed-in user can read another customer’s invoice by changing a number in the URL. There is no injection and no unsafe call. Nothing in the code matches a known bad pattern.

The fix is rarely long, but it is hard to get right. You need to know how your application identifies the caller, where ownership lives in your data model, and how the rest of the codebase already enforces it. Get that wrong and you either leave the hole open or break a legitimate workflow. So these findings often wait for whoever knows the access model best.

How does the Remediation Agent fix a Hunter Agent finding?

It starts from a finding that has already been checked. Hunter Agent tests each candidate to rule out false positives. It then raises the finding as a vulnerability with a severity, an exact location in the code, and an explanation in two parts: why it is an issue, and how to fix it. The Remediation Agent works from that finding and from your full repository, not just the lines that were flagged.

The workflow is the one your team may already use for backlog fixes:

  1. Open your project’s Issues page and select the main branch.
  2. Turn on the Fixable by Agent filter. Eligible Hunter Agent findings appear alongside your other fixable issues. To see only Hunter Agent findings, add the hunter-agent tag, or a category tag such as hunter-broken-access-control.
  3. Select the findings you want fixed, up to 20 at a time, and choose Fix with Agent.
  4. Follow the run on the Remediation Agent page.
  5. When a fix is available, open the linked pull request, review it, and merge it.

The agent generates each change through your organization’s own OpenAI or Anthropic key, and verifies the proposed change before it opens a pull request.

Why does each finding get its own pull request?

For rule-based issues, the agent groups the fixes you assign by rule key and file type. Hunter Agent findings are handled differently. Each finding gets its own pull request, or merge request on Github, when a fix is available.

That fits security work. One pull request maps to one finding. items.title: Patient records exposed in Quest breach: What you need to know
items.summary: Quest Diagnostics has confirmed that an unauthorized party accessed a system healthcare providers use to order laboratory tests and view results, affecting personal information and patient records. Quest is a major US laboratory testing company whose services help healthcare professionals diagnose and monitor medical conditions. Those services range from routine laboratory testing to specialized testing in areas such as cancer, infectious diseases, and neurology. What happened and what was stolen? The company learned of unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, or LSM, on October 21. The compromised platform lets healthcare professionals order tests, access results, review historical trends, and order supplies. Quest paused access to the platform and began investigating. Quest says its core business operations remain up and running. An investigation is ongoing. Quest has not yet published a count of affected patients or a complete list of the information accessed. It says it will notify affected patients, healthcare providers, and health plans. The company said: “personal information and patient records were affected.” It confirms that health information and personally identifiable information were involved, but has not specified whether these included Social Security numbers, insurance identifiers, payment information, particular test results, or account passwords. What patients can do now Quest says it will send notification letters to affected patients once its investigation is complete. Those letters will describe available resources, including credit and identity monitoring. If you receive one, read it carefully and follow the instructions. You can also check the FAQs posted in Quest’s breach notice for updates. Someone’s watching your accounts. Make sure it’s us. PROTECT YOUR IDENTITY A breach does not automatically mean someone has misused your information, but you can take these precautions while you wait for more details: Verify unexpected messages independently. Don’t let a message about the breach rush you into clicking a link, sharing sensitive information, or making a payment. Go to Quest’s official website yourself or use contact details you already trust. Review medical bills and insurance statements. Look for appointments, tests, prescriptions, or services you did not receive. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) identifies unfamiliar medical bills and unexpected items on an Explanation of Benefits statement, which explains how your insurer processed a claim, as warning signs of medical identity theft. Report discrepancies to your healthcare provider and your insurer. Review your credit reports. Look for unfamiliar accounts or debts and dispute errors. Free reports are available through AnnualCreditReport.com . Act if you find signs of identity theft. Visit IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan. If someone has received care in your name, ask the providers involved for copies of your medical records and request corrections in writing. Medical identity theft is not just a financial problem; it can also affect your care. Someone using your identity to obtain treatment or submit insurance claims could introduce incorrect information into your health records. Checking medical statements and reporting anything unfamiliar can help you catch that misuse. Let’s face it, an incognito window can only do so much. Breaches, dark web trading, credit fraud. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection monitors for all of it, alerts you fast, and comes with identity theft insurance.

items.title: Isolation. Security. Scale.
items.summary: Without these three things, Agents cannot be properly implemented in a controlled environment, they will not have policy enforcement to ensure they do what they’re supposed to do, and there’s zero way of ensuring that the Agent will be readily available when needed. Kagent as the runtime for declarative and BYO (covering frameworks like langgraph/ADK) Agents combined with Agent Substrate for the underlying sandbox environment ensures that you can implement all three production-level needs when running agentic workloads. In this blog post, you’ll learn the key concepts to agent sandboxing, how Substrate is used, and implementing it with kagent. Prerequisites To follow along with this blog post in a hands-on fashion, you will need: A Kubernetes cluster (local cluster like Kind or Minikube is fine). If you do not have a k8s cluster, you can follow along from a theoretical perspective for the learnings until you have a cluster readily available. Agent sandboxing as a whole If you spin up Docker or whatever containerization engine you prefer, create a container, and run a workload in it, technically speaking the workload is “sandboxed”. However, that level of sandboxing might as well not even exist. Ingress and egress is wide open, the workload can send packets to whatever it likes, and there’s zero policy enforcement. Of course there are ways to tighten this up (network policies, segmentation, routing rules, etc.), but that doesn’t change the fact that sandboxing as a whole is “flat” by nature. Sandboxing an Agent in a secure and effective fashion means: Untrusted agent code cannot escape into the host environment or compromise underlying infrastructure. The blast radius for a harness is minimized. The Agent that holds onto model output, possibility credentials, and tool calls is within an isolated boundary. Agents are snapshotted so it knows where to pick up where it left off (where the state exists). Agent multiplexing (routing traffic to multiple Agents) in a multi-tenant environment is isolated and has a boundary. To ensure that the above can be properly implemented, you need the ability to isolate Agents at both the hardware and software level along with policy enforcement at the AI Gateway for when Agent traffic is reaching its destination. Where does agent substrate fit In? Container isolation (and software-level isolation to that point) stops at your kernel. Everything is running in said kernel (in the user space), which can be sufficient for some, but how that isolation is implemented matters. How the client routes to the Agent and what is in the middle facilitating that routing is what counts when it comes to isolation. That’s where Agent Substrate comes into play. With Agent Substrate, all Agents are running in Workers, which are Pods. The Agents are facilitated via Actors, which are managed by the ateapi (Agent Substrate’s Control Plane). Where the isolation comes into play is with software and hardware-level isolation. gVisor is used for software-level isolation and microVM is used for hardware-level isolation. With software-level isolation, the isolated workload runs inside of the user space using a dedicated user-space app kernel called Sentry that intercepts and handles system calls. MicroVM guest OS/VM runs directly on physical CPU cores using hardware-level virtualization extensions. Running in the user space/namespace (e.g., software level isolation) is a decision for the system, like gVisor. Using substrate in Kagent In the previous sections, you learned about the architecture, design, and system choices for why sandboxing an Agent is important. In the upcoming sections, you’ll learn how to do it in a hands-on fashion with kagent and Agent Substrate. The interaction points you’ll see where is; kagent is the runtime, Agent Substrate is the platform sitting understand to help implement and facilitate sandboxing. Without kagent, the only real entry point to interact with Agent Substrate is via a programmatic call with something like a curl to interact with the Actor. Kagent allows you to interact with Agents running in Actors via Substrate in a way that the industry is comfortable with (a UI and in a declarative fashion). Installation and Configuration There are a few steps to installing kagent v1.0 and Agent Substrate, including: Configuring kubectl-ate (to interact with Agent Substrate via the CLI). The installation of Agent Substrate itself Installing kagent To get a play-by-play, step-by-step instruction set, you can take a look at the guide found here . Once you’re up and running, you’ll see that with the Helm installation of kagent by default, one WorkerPool gets created with two Workers (Pods). The WorkerPool gets created with the substrateWorkerPool.create= true setting on the Helm Chart. Creating an agent programmatically With kagent + Agent Substrate installed, you can now create an Agent (Actor) and an Agent Template. The AgentTemplate is like a “golden image” (although, “image” feels a bit too heavy of wording) that contains the configurations for your Agent and can be reused across Agents that you deploy. The Harness is the Actor (Agent) itself. This can be something like a Harness (Codex, Claude Code, etc.) or a BYO Agent using a framework like langgraph. Run the below to declaratively create the Harness and AgentTemplate using the kagent CRDs. kubectl apply -f - < Once deployed, you’ll see the Agent running in kagent along with the template. Creating an agent in the UI Aside from creating an Agent in a declarative fashion, you can also create one in the UI. Within the UI, click on the Agents pane. Click the purple + New template button. You can then define the template like how you did in the YAML within the previous section. Go into the Harness configuration via the purple + New Harness section. Within there is where you can define the harness like you did declaratively in the previous section to point to the Namespace that you want the Actor/Agent deployed in, the name, runtime adapter, and the location where the image exists. Using a sandboxed agent When you open the Agents tab, you’ll see the `assistant` Agent. Then, go over to the Substrate tab. Notice how it says 0/8 Actors running? That’s because an Actor is only running when there’s an active session (this ties back to the efficiency of hardware resources when using Agent Substrate) Next, open your Agent and prompt it with whatever you’d like. You’ll now see that there are 0/9 Actors. The reason why is because when you start a new session, a new Actor spins up. It then spins down once the session is complete (the session being what you’re asking the Agent and when it responds). If you open a new session and prompt the Agent, you’ll see 0/10. If you use an existing session, the Actor count won’t change because it’s still the same session. This is important because it can look like “every time I use an Agent, a new Actor spins up and that’s a lot of resources to manage”, but it’s only when a new session occurs. Wrapping Up In this section, you not only learned about why sandboxing is important and the key projects driving sandboxing forward, but how to deploy Actors within kagent using Agent Substrate as the sandbox platform/architecture. Moving forward for engineering teams and enterprises alike, having the ability to isolate, secure, govern, and control Agents will be key to truly understanding what your Agents can and can’t do, which is a key holding point today for many organizations when implementing Agents.

items.summary: Interesting research : TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it. One word tilts the code against Americans. Ask for the app “for a US defense contractor” instead of “for a Chinese defense contractor”, and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked. Hong Kong’s democracy movement gets apps that leak. Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else’s secrets. Asking for secure code didn’t help. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor’s apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer’s. Westernized Qwen3-Coder closed all three gaps. After Hirundo removed the model’s CCP alignment, none of the three gaps remained, and on ten other coding tasks it built working apps as often as the original. It is available on Hugging Face . I would like more details on how the bias was removed.

items.title: Kali Linux 2026.3 Released With 6 New Penetration Testing Tools and Linux Kernel 7.1
items.summary: Kali Linux 2026.3 has been released as the third Kali update of 2026, bringing six new penetration testing tools, Linux kernel 7.1.5, KDE Plasma 6.7, refreshed image-building scripts, and a large set of Kali NetHunter changes. The release arrived on October 26 with 126 package updates and moves the kernel from version 6.19 to 7.1.5. The update follows June’s Kali Linux 2026.2 release , which added nine tools, changed Kali’s APT source format, and improved virtual machine boot times. It also continues the tool and mobile testing work seen in Kali Linux 2026.1 , the first major Kali update of the year. Six New Penetration Testing Tools The six new tools are available from Kali’s network repositories. Dalfox is an open-source cross-site scripting scanner built for automation and parameter checks. Katana is a crawling and spidering framework that can help researchers map web applications and find paths, files, and endpoints before deeper testing. Qsreplace takes URLs from standard input and replaces query string values with a chosen value, which makes it useful for preparing URL lists for repeatable web tests. Rustscan is a fast port scanner written in Rust. It can scan large port ranges and pass discovered ports to Nmap for deeper service checks. SDRangel is a Qt-based software-defined radio front end that supports devices such as RTL-SDR, BladeRF, and HackRF, giving wireless researchers a visual tool for receiving, sending, and studying radio signals. Tool Main purpose Key use Dalfox Automated XSS scanner Finds and verifies cross-site scripting flaws by testing web parameters. Katana Web crawling and spidering Maps websites, parses JavaScript, finds endpoints, and supports standard or headless crawling. Qsreplace Query-string replacement Reads URLs from standard input and replaces their query values for repeatable web security tests. Rustscan Fast network port scanner Finds open ports quickly and can pass the results to Nmap for deeper checks. SDRangel Software-defined radio interface Provides a graphical front end for radio devices such as RTL-SDR, BladeRF, and HackRF. Snaffler-ng SMB data scanner Searches readable Windows SMB shares for exposed credentials and sensitive files. Snaffler-ng searches readable Windows SMB shares for credentials and sensitive data. It supports NTLM and Kerberos sign-in, DFS discovery, archive checks, built-in classification rules, SQLite resume support, and several output formats. These additions cover web discovery, XSS testing, URL processing, port scanning, radio research, and file-share review. Like any security tool, they should only be used on systems that the tester owns or has clear permission to assess. Linux Kernel 7.1.5 and Package Updates Kali 2026.3 contains 126 package updates and moves the main Kali kernel from 6.19 to 7.1.5. Kali’s package tracker lists 7.1.5-1kali1 for the rolling branch, confirming the kernel used by the new release. The newer kernel matters because it provides the base for hardware support, drivers, system calls, and security fixes used by the rest of the distribution. Users should still test wireless adapters, graphics drivers, virtualization tools, and any custom kernel modules before relying on the update during live security work. One of the largest changes is the refresh of Kali’s public build scripts. These are the same scripts the project uses to create the official images offered through its download site. The refreshed scripts now have a more consistent structure, layout, command-line options, features, and output across supported platforms. Each refreshed project includes a build-in-container.sh script. It detects whether Docker or Podman is present, creates a build container, and runs the image build inside that container. This removes the earlier need to build Kali on a Kali system and makes the process easier to repeat on other Debian-based hosts. Kali has also improved its related build documentation. Users who want to build a standard installer can clone the kali-installer build repository, install the required packages, and run sudo ./build.sh . The default command creates a Kali rolling installer for AMD64. Builders can change the hostname, add packages such as Rustscan, select kali-dev , choose a netinst image, or target ARM64 through command-line options. Podman users can instead install Podman and run sudo ./build-in-container.sh . The work is not finished. Kali says some build scripts did not make the 2026.3 deadline, and the remaining refresh is planned for Kali 2026.4. Later stages are expected to focus on automated builds, workflows, example setups, and deeper customization. Teams with CI jobs based on the older scripts should review their pipelines because changes made during the refresh may have broken older workflows. KDE Plasma 6.7 and New Icons The optional KDE desktop has been updated to Plasma 6.7. A key feature is per-screen virtual desktops, which lets users change the workspace on one monitor without changing every display. This can be useful when keeping Burp Suite on one screen, terminals on another, and notes or documentation on a third. Plasma’s Overview also supports faster desktop switching by scrolling or using Page Up and Page Down. KDE Plasma 6.7 adds more Wayland protocol and portal support, better performance and lower power use for integrated Intel graphics, CPU-rendered applications, and setups with many full-screen windows. Network connections can be duplicated, while System Monitor, software management, printing, background application display, microphone testing, and desktop search controls also receive changes. KDE has added a light and dark theme switch, improved Breeze, restored the Oxygen and Air styles, and introduced an early preview of its Union theming system. Kali has also added icons to tools that did not have them and updated older icons so applications are easier to identify in the menu and on the Kali tools website. Xfce remains Kali’s default desktop even though KDE received the main desktop version change in this release. Major Kali NetHunter Changes Kali NetHunter, the project’s Android and wearable security testing platform, receives some of the release’s most unusual changes. The team addressed compatibility problems between modern systemd and udev components and older mobile kernels without requiring large sets of patches. Wardriving is now supported on the TicWatch Pro 3 series. An updated libnexmonkali library enables internal Wi-Fi monitor mode on the watch, allowing compatible tools inside the Kali chroot, including Aircrack-ng and Kismet, to work with the watch’s wireless hardware. Kali’s TicWatch guide says all Pro 3 GPS, LTE, Ultra GPS, and Ultra LTE variants are supported, though installation requires bootloader, recovery, operating system, root, and NetHunter changes. WearHunter is a new experimental feature that lets a user control a NetHunter watch from a phone through ADB over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. It can run commands and install applications, with more functions planned. NFC Arsenal now provides NFC access to the Kali chroot and can read, clone, and edit Mifare Classic cards without an external adapter. The release also adds KernelSU support, allowing a generated installer ZIP to be installed through the KernelSU application when used with a patched kernel. Other NetHunter work includes a fix for TicWatch Pro 3 reboot problems and early support for devices that do not use a ramdisk. Bluetooth Arsenal’s airplane mode has returned. EvilTwin and Wardriving are easier to start, while custom commands now support Nexmon monitor mode and Wifite. Kali also fixed a crash caused by the NetHunter application’s storage request and delivered other bug fixes and speed improvements. Nine new device kernels were added. They cover Google Pixel on LineageOS 22.2 with Android 15, Huawei P9 on EMUI 8 or LineageOS 16, LG K20 Plus on LineageOS 14.1, Moto G Stylus 5G 2022 on LineageOS 23.2, Nubia Z17 on LineageOS 22.2, POCO X5 5G and Redmi Note 12 5G on crDroid 12, Redmi Note 5 Pro on LineageOS 18.1, Sony Xperia 10 V on LineageOS 23.2, and Ulefone Armor 34+ on Android 16. The release announcement also highlighted the Wardriver Project, a 2021 Honda Civic Type R shown at the Cars and Cops event in Altus, Oklahoma. The project was used to show how vehicle culture, wireless research, and cybersecurity can meet in a single build. Website and Documentation Updates Kali has applied the category layout and icons introduced in its desktop menu to kali.org/tools . Users who prefer the older short view can still open the Top 100 tools page. The documentation set gains three new pages. They explain how to extract and squash vendor firmware for mainline Linux, import a pre-made Kali QEMU virtual machine, and use NetHunter EvilTwin. Nine existing guides were updated, covering Live USB persistence, graphics problems on bare-metal systems, NetHunter on the TicWatch Pro 3, Kali as a UTM guest, the Xfce FAQ, Kali NetHunter, Raspberry Pi full-disk encryption, setting up a Kali mirror, and SSH configuration. The release cycle also added four European mirrors. Two are in the Netherlands at mirror.hacker.nl and mirror.netone.nl . Portugal gained mirror.randhost.com , while Switzerland gained kalimirror.velden.media . Kali’s mirror system can direct users to a nearby current server, but its documentation warns against adding extra repositories to the Kali source configuration because mixing repositories can break an installation. Kali also thanked community members who worked on documentation, tool pages, NetHunter, and package maintenance. The long contributor list reflects how much of the mobile kernel, device, documentation, and packaging work comes from outside contributors rather than only the core Kali team. Downloading and Upgrading Kali 2026.3 New users can obtain tested installer, live, virtual machine, ARM, cloud, container, and NetHunter images from the official Kali download page . Kali recommends the latest point-release image for most users. Weekly images contain newer packages and can reduce the number of updates needed after installation, but they are automated and do not receive the same quality checks as standard point-release images. Existing rolling users should first confirm that /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kali.sources points to the official kali-rolling repository with the main , contrib , non-free , and non-free-firmware components. They can then run sudo apt update followed by sudo apt full-upgrade -y . If the system marks a reboot as required, users should restart before checking the result. The installed release can be checked with grep VERSION /etc/os-release , which should show 2026.3 . The active kernel can be checked with uname -r , with the AMD64 release example showing 7.1.5+kali-amd64 . The exact kernel string can differ by architecture. Kali’s update guidance recommends checking for updates every few days or weeks, or sooner when a required tool or security fix is released. It also advises testing all needed tools before a planned security engagement and avoiding updates during active work because a rolling package change can sometimes break a tool at the wrong time Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Builders can change the hostname, add packages such as Rustscan, select kali-dev, choose a netinst image, or target ARM64 through command-line options. Podman users can instead install Podman and run sudo ./build-in-container.sh.

The work is not finished. Kali says some build scripts did not make the 2026.3 deadline, and the remaining refresh is planned for Kali 2026.4. Later stages are expected to focus on automated builds, workflows, example setups, and deeper customization. Teams with CI jobs based on the older scripts should review their pipelines because changes made during the refresh may have broken older workflows.

KDE Plasma 6.7 and New Icons

The optional KDE desktop has been updated to Plasma 6.7. A key feature is per-screen virtual desktops, which lets users change the workspace on one monitor without changing every display.

This can be useful when keeping Burp Suite on one screen, terminals on another, and notes or documentation on a third. Plasma’s Overview also supports faster desktop switching by scrolling or using Page Up and Page Down.

KDE Plasma 6.7 adds more Wayland protocol and portal support, better performance and lower power use for integrated Intel graphics, CPU-rendered applications, and setups with many full-screen windows. Network connections can be duplicated, while System Monitor, software management, printing, background application display, microphone testing, and desktop search controls also receive changes.

KDE has added a light and dark theme switch, improved Breeze, restored the Oxygen and Air styles, and introduced an early preview of its Union theming system.

Kali has also added icons to tools that did not have them and updated older icons so applications are easier to identify in the menu and on the Kali tools website. Xfce remains Kali’s default desktop even though KDE received the main desktop version change in this release.

Major Kali NetHunter Changes

Kali NetHunter, the project’s Android and wearable security testing platform, receives some of the release’s most unusual changes. The team addressed compatibility problems between modern systemd and udev components and older mobile kernels without requiring large sets of patches.

Wardriving is now supported on the TicWatch Pro 3 series. An updated libnexmonkali library enables internal Wi-Fi monitor mode on the watch, allowing compatible tools inside the Kali chroot, including Aircrack-ng and Kismet, to work with the watch’s wireless hardware. Kali’s TicWatch guide says all Pro 3 GPS, LTE, Ultra GPS, and Ultra LTE variants are supported, though installation requires bootloader, recovery, operating system, root, and NetHunter changes.

WearHunter is a new experimental feature that lets a user control a NetHunter watch from a phone through ADB over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. It can run commands and install applications, with more functions planned. NFC Arsenal now provides NFC access to the Kali chroot and can read, clone, and edit Mifare Classic cards without an external adapter. The release also adds KernelSU support, allowing a generated installer ZIP to be installed through the KernelSU application when used with a patched kernel.

Other NetHunter work includes a fix for TicWatch Pro 3 reboot problems and early support for devices that do not use a ramdisk. Bluetooth Arsenal’s airplane mode has returned. EvilTwin and Wardriving are easier to start, while custom commands now support Nexmon monitor mode and Wifite. Kali also fixed a crash caused by the NetHunter application’s storage request and delivered other bug fixes and speed improvements.

Nine new device kernels were added. They cover Google Pixel on LineageOS 22.2 with Android 15, Huawei P9 on EMUI 8 or LineageOS 16, LG K20 Plus on LineageOS 14.1, Moto G Stylus 5G 2022 on LineageOS 23.2, Nubia Z17 on LineageOS 22.2, POCO X5 5G and Redmi Note 12 5G on crDroid 12, Redmi Note 5 Pro on LineageOS 18.1, Sony Xperia 10 V on LineageOS 23.2, and Ulefone Armor 34+ on Android 16.

The release announcement also highlighted the Wardriver Project, a 2021 Honda Civic Type R shown at the Cars and Cops event in Altus, Oklahoma. The project was used to show how vehicle culture, wireless research, and cybersecurity can meet in a single build.

Website and Documentation Updates

Kali has applied the category layout and icons introduced in its desktop menu to kali.org/tools. Users who prefer the older short view can still open the Top 100 tools page.

The documentation set gains three new pages. They explain how to extract and squash vendor firmware for mainline Linux, import a pre-made Kali QEMU virtual machine, and use NetHunter EvilTwin.

Nine existing guides were updated, covering Live USB persistence, graphics problems on bare-metal systems, NetHunter on the TicWatch Pro 3, Kali as a UTM guest, the Xfce FAQ, Kali NetHunter, Raspberry Pi full-disk encryption, setting up a Kali mirror, and SSH configuration.

The release cycle also added four European mirrors. Two are in the Netherlands at mirror.hacker.nl and mirror.netone.nl. Portugal gained mirror.randhost.com, while Switzerland gained kalimirror.velden.media. Kali’s mirror system can direct users to a nearby current server, but its documentation warns against adding extra repositories to the Kali source configuration because mixing repositories can break an installation.

Kali also thanked community members who worked on documentation, tool pages, NetHunter, and package maintenance. The long contributor list reflects how much of the mobile kernel, device, documentation, and packaging work comes from outside contributors rather than only the core Kali team.

Downloading and Upgrading Kali 2026.3

New users can obtain tested installer, live, virtual machine, ARM, cloud, container, and NetHunter images from the official Kali download page. Kali recommends the latest point-release image for most users. Weekly images contain newer packages and can reduce the number of updates needed after installation, but they are automated and do not receive the same quality checks as standard point-release images.

Existing rolling users should first confirm that /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kali.sources points to the official kali-rolling repository with the main, contrib, non-free, and non-free-firmware components. They can then run sudo apt update followed by sudo apt full-upgrade -y. If the system marks a reboot as required, users should restart before checking the result.

The installed release can be checked with grep VERSION /etc/os-release, which should show 2026.3. The active kernel can be checked with uname -r, with the AMD64 release example showing 7.1.5+kali-amd64. The exact kernel string can differ by architecture.

Kali’s update guidance recommends checking for updates every few days or weeks, or sooner when a required tool or security fix is released. It also advises testing all needed tools before a planned security engagement and avoiding updates during active work because a rolling package change can sometimes break a tool at the wrong time

items.summary: OpenSSL has released version 4.1.0, bringing DTLS 1.3 support, faster cryptographic operations, and new tools for developers building secure network services. Published on October 23, the update is a feature release, not a standalone security patch. It also includes compatibility changes and four known issues that teams should review before deployment. The official release notes identify DTLS 1.3 as a key addition. The release follows the earlier OpenSSL 4.1.0 Alpha1 preview , which introduced the protocol alongside GREASE support and cryptographic performance improvements. Datagram Transport Layer Security protects applications that use transports such as UDP. Unlike TCP, UDP does not guarantee that packets arrive or arrive in order. DTLS adds encryption and authentication while preserving that behavior, making it useful for applications where delays matter, including gaming and some streaming services. OpenSSL 4.1.0 Released With DTLS 1.3 Defined in RFC 9147, DTLS 1.3 builds on TLS 1.3 and helps prevent eavesdropping, data tampering, and forged messages. It provides similar security guarantees, but applications must account for differences in message ordering and replay protection. DTLS also handles lost handshake messages without turning application traffic into a reliable, ordered stream. OpenSSL 4.1.0 adds DTLS support to its SSL listener API. Other additions include GREASE, the IKEv2 key derivation function, and initial support for the Elbrus2000 processor architecture. GREASE stands for Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility. The release improves ML-DSA and ML-KEM number theoretic transform operations on ppc64le systems. On x86_64, it adds optimized ML-DSA operations, AVX-512 SHAKE processing for ML-DSA, and AVX-512 and VAES improvements for AES-CBC decryption. The release notes provide no benchmark figures. Developers using the tsget utility must install Net::Curl::Easy before upgrading because it replaces the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy dependency. OpenSSL also removes Windows-on-Itanium and Windows CE build targets while adding targets that address gaps in MSVC 2013’s C99 support. The no-ecdsa and no-ecdh configuration options have been removed because they didn’t actually turn off those implementations. Teams seeking to turn off elliptic curve support must use no-ec instead. Four documented problems affect DTLS behavior. Receiving a DTLS 1.3 KeyUpdate can remove other pending post-handshake records from the retransmission buffer. If the original packets are lost, records such as session tickets will not be resent. A fix is planned for a future release. Listener error handling also has limitations. A permanent receive failure may appear as SSL_ERROR_WANT_READ, leaving applications waiting. A retryable write failure may instead appear as SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL, potentially causing applications to close usable connections. items.title: HTTP2Shell Vulnerability Extends Beyond HTTP, Affecting .NET, FFmpeg, ClickHouse, and Apache Arrow
items.summary: The HTTP2Shell vulnerability reaches beyond web traffic, with new research showing how the same Brotli decoder flaw (CVE-2026-111497) can disrupt .NET applications, FFmpeg media processing, ClickHouse servers, and Apache Arrow workloads. The findings show that checking Node.js versions alone can leave other exposed software unnoticed. In research published on October 25, JFrog researchers Aviv Engelberg, Eddy Tsalolikhin, and Ofri Ouzan traced CVE-2026-111497 through several software stacks. Their findings describe crashes, memory corruption, and an endless decoding loop, depending on how each application uses the affected library. First disclosed in Node.js security updates on October 21, the vulnerability sits in Google’s Brotli decoder rather than HTTP itself. An invalid block switch can be mistaken for a request for more input. Processing then continues with broken decoder state, allowing a write beyond the intended memory buffer. Affected upstream releases include Brotli 1.0.3 through versions before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. Projects may apply the fix without changing to these upstream versions, so teams must check vendor patch records rather than relying on version numbers alone. HTTP2Shell Vulnerability In FFmpeg, researchers reached the decoder through libjxl, which processes JPEG XL images. A crafted image carried malformed Brotli data inside a compressed metadata box. When libjxl decoded that data, memory corruption caused a crash during cleanup. The test showed attacker control over a corrupted pointer value. However, it did not establish a complete remote code execution exploit for FFmpeg. This file-based route adds to concerns covered in earlier reporting on FFmpeg media-file vulnerabilities and other FFmpeg memory-corruption flaws . Those reports concern separate vulnerabilities. JFrog also triggered a native crash through .NET’s Brotli decompression APIs. A two-stage stream left the decoder in an invalid state before a memory operation moved outside valid heap data. Unlike a normal managed exception, the resulting segmentation fault terminated the process. The demonstration used a local console application. However, related decoder paths can serve HttpClient response decompression and ASP.NET Core request-decompression middleware. Microsoft announced on October 25 that it was rolling out updates for supported runtimes and SDKs. ClickHouse failed after receiving one crafted HTTP request with a 23 MB Brotli-compressed body. Decoder corruption caused a crash during cleanup, stopping the tested server and interrupting active queries. JFrog reported that a fix had been merged, but no patched release had shipped when its research appeared. Apache Arrow showed a different failure. A 534-byte input sent through pyarrow’s Brotli decoding path caused an endless loop that consumed CPU and blocked completion. Brotli 1.2.1 rejected the same input in under a second. items.title: Microsoft Authenticator Flaw Lets Malicious Android Apps Steal Account Tokens With Zero Permissions
items.summary: Microsoft patched high-severity flaw CVE-2026-80097 (CVSS 8.6) in Authenticator for Android, allowing malicious apps with no declared permissions to steal work account access tokens due to improper authentication in its broker component. Microsoft classified the flaw as a local elevation-of-privilege vulnerability. The issue affected Android devices with Microsoft Authenticator installed and a signed-in work account. Enclave researchers found that an untrusted app could pretend to be a trusted Microsoft application, such as Microsoft Teams, and ask Authenticator to issue delegated tokens for that identity. The request did not need user approval, account credentials, or Android permissions beyond being installed on the device. At the center of the bug was an exported Android activity named com.microsoft.identity.client.AccountChooserActivity. Other apps can start exported activities on the same device. In this case, the activity accepted a broker request from the calling app. It returned the authentication result after processing it. The key problem was how Authenticator verified the requesting application. The broker request included the claimed app package name, client ID, redirect URI, requested scopes, and even a caller UID value. Microsoft Authenticator Flaw Enclave researchers reported that the malicious application could supply these fields rather than having them tied to the app that actually launched the request. Authenticator did perform a signature-related redirect URI validation. However, the check focused on the app identity claimed in the request. If the attacker claimed to be Teams, the vulnerable logic checked whether the redirect URI matched the real installed Teams package. Because Teams was legitimately installed, the attacker could build a valid redirect URI from its public package signature and pass the check. In short, the app verified whether the claimed identity looked valid, but did not confirm that the real caller was the app it claimed to be. The vulnerable activity could identify the package that launched it, according to the research. However, it did not use that information to control trust. Successful requests returned token data through the activity result bundle. The tokens could include access tokens, refresh tokens, ID tokens, and client information. Depending on the impersonated Microsoft client and requested permissions, the impact could extend to Microsoft Graph resources such as mailboxes, calendars, OneDrive files, SharePoint content, and Teams-related services. The researchers demonstrated the risk by impersonating multiple Microsoft apps. A Teams identity requesting Microsoft Graph access could receive delegated permissions that let it read and write mail, send messages, access files, and modify calendars. This flaw is especially important for organizations that use Android devices to access Microsoft 365 workloads. Microsoft fixed the issue in Microsoft Authenticator for Android version 6.2606.4246, which was released in July 2026. Organizations and individual users should update the app through Google Play as soon as possible and verify that managed devices are running a current release. Microsoft’s advisory describes the issue as improper authentication that could let an unauthorized local attacker elevate privileges. The flaw also highlights why mobile identity brokers must validate the real calling application, including its package identity, UID, and signing certificate, rather than relying on app-controlled values in an intent. The incident highlights Microsoft’s ongoing efforts to protect Entra credentials on rooted Android and jailbroken iOS devices , where malware and weakened security controls increase enterprise identity risks. Organizations should review mobile application controls, enforce timely app updates through MDM or EMM platforms, and restrict sideloaded applications where possible. Security teams should also monitor unusual Microsoft Graph activity, unexpected consent behavior, and token use from unfamiliar Android devices. Microsoft’s official CVE-2026-80097 advisory should be used for ongoing remediation guidance. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: India’s Film Sensor Board Data Breach – Unreleased Scripts, 500+ Film Titles Exposed
items.summary: India’s Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) is investigating a reported data breach involving confidential documents linked to more than 500 film titles. The exposed records reportedly include shooting scripts, censor cut orders, certification files and private distribution agreements submitted through its e-Cinepramaan portal. The Hindu first reported the exposure, which involved film certification applications rather than leaked movie files. Its reporting describes more than 500 affected titles, including dozens of feature films. That distinction matters because the incident does not mean 500 complete films or 500 separate scripts were stolen. Film Scripts and Business Records Exposed Filmmakers use e-Cinepramaan to submit documents needed for certification before theatrical release. According to reports, the files were allegedly accessed through this portal and remained available online for several days before removal. The material reportedly appeared on the Internet Archive, where it could be downloaded. Documents dated from December 2025 to August 2026 were among the exposed records, according to Digit’s coverage of the findings. The commercial impact could extend beyond spoilers. Local distribution agreements for The Secret Agent and Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die were reportedly included. At least three agreements disclosed licensing fees, potentially revealing private deal terms to competitors or future negotiating partners. For unreleased productions, exposed scripts could reveal storylines before marketing campaigns begin. Cut orders could also disclose scenes removed during certification. These are potential consequences of the reported exposure, not confirmed cases of financial loss or misuse. The CBFC has reportedly started an investigation and a security audit. The board said its initial checks had not found evidence of further access to the documents identified in the report. It also said there was no indication that individual filmmakers’ accounts had been compromised. According to India Today’s coverage , uploads stopped after the portal became unavailable for several hours on October 4. That timing alone does not establish how access occurred or whether the outage stopped it. The Internet Archive reportedly removed the account involved. Cybercrime authorities received a complaint, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, CERT-In, was notified. The investigation has not yet established the full exposure. The available reporting does not identify a confirmed software flaw or access method. Cyber Security News previously covered an Indian Post Office portal document exposure involving broken access controls, but there is no evidence linking that weakness to CBFC. Similarly, its SBI data breach coverage separated exposed records from an unconfirmed entry point. For CBFC, the key unanswered questions remain how documents became accessible, which submissions were affected, and whether copies remain elsewhere. Until investigators publish findings, claims of stolen passwords, ransomware or a specific vulnerability remain unsupported by the available public reporting. items.title: Can’t Patch PHP2Shell Yet? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
items.summary: PHP2Shell comes with a clear instruction: update PHP. Fixed releases exist for supported branches, and Qualys customers can identify PHP installations using network scans, Cloud Agents, container assessments, and Deep Scan where supported, while assessing exposed web applications and APIs with Qualys TotalAppSec. Patching at this scale still takes time. In Qualys telemetry, only 199,000 of the 156 million PHP package installations with a known version had been patched during the first 12 hours after disclosure. Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while updates roll out, and the right visibility shows which servers need attention first. Our PHP2Shell guide covers detection and fixed versions. Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and patch. Start with Qualys Mitigation Qualys provides a configuration-level mitigation for PHP2Shell based on PHP’s guidance and insights from the Qualys Threat Research Unit. It disables session upload progress and hardens related session-handling configuration on supported hosts. This reduces exposure to the confirmed session-lifecycle attack path without requiring application-code changes. It does not eliminate every exploitation path associated with the two CVEs. Applications that depend on upload-progress functionality should be tested after the change. Configuration-level, with restart verification . The mitigation applies configuration changes and automatically restarts the PHP service. Review the execution logs and restart the service manually if a restart is still required. Confirm that every affected PHP worker has picked up the new configuration. Verified, not assumed. After the restart, Qualys checks the effective configuration to confirm the setting is active and not overridden elsewhere. With or without an agent. Customers with vulnerable detections can select Mitigate Now from their dashboards. For appliances, DMZ servers, and legacy hosts that cannot run a Cloud Agent, the same mitigation script is available in the Custom Assessment and Remediation (CAR) library in TruRisk Eliminate and runs directly on scanner-based hosts. Ready when the patch is. You can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate. Qualys reports a High patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for this PHP package update. Restart every service that loads PHP and verify that its workers are running the patched build. Mitigation reduces risk in the interim. Updating remains the only complete fix. Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run The tools already in your environment can work alongside the mitigation, each at a different point in the attack path. Network and application protection: WAF and IPS. Vendors including Akamai, Cloudflare, F5, Palo Alto Networks, Fortinet, and Check Point have published PHP2Shell protections. Coverage varies by product, CVE, signature, and configuration. These protections can block known exploit requests; some, including Cloudflare’s, also inspect and block malicious responses. Keep signatures current and confirm that the relevant traffic is inspected and blocking is enabled. Cloudflare has reported attempts to bypass its protections, so treat these controls as additional layers while patching proceeds. After exploitation: EDR. Endpoint controls can provide visibility into suspicious child processes, malicious command execution, and web-shell deployment. CrowdStrike Falcon and Cortex XDR document PHP2Shell-related post-exploitation protections. For Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and other tools, verify the applicable platform support and enabled policies before claiming specific coverage. These layers can detect or block different stages of an attack, but they do not guarantee that every exploitation attempt will be stopped. Each layer catches what the one before it might miss.   3. Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate, from the platform that found the exposure.

Validate the Tested Entry Point with TruConfirm

TruConfirm helps validate indicators of the tested PHP2Shell entry point. According to Qualys’s PHP2Shell guide, its benign probe checks for behavior indicating that the entry point is reachable and the upload-progress mitigation is absent, without creating files, executing code, or applying memory pressure.

Qualys reports that, in one customer environment with 1,539 assets running PHP, TruConfirm returned positive validation results for 25 assets. These findings help prioritize investigation and remediation. A negative result does not establish that every exploitation path is closed. After mitigation or patching, repeat the validation and separately verify the effective configuration, installed packages, and running PHP workers.

Where to Start
  1. Use QID 45110 to support PHP discovery, then use the applicable vulnerability detection QIDs and software inventory to assess assets in scope.
  2. Use TruConfirm results alongside internet exposure and business criticality to prioritize remediation.
  3. Apply the supported Qualys mitigation workflow to systems awaiting an update, using agent-based or scanner-based execution as applicable.
  4. Verify the effective configuration and required restarts.Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers.
  5. Deploy the appropriate PHP or vendor update, restart every service that loads PHP, verify the running patched build, and repeat the relevant validation checks.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

The public script uses two memory leaks. The first leak reveals a heap address, and the second reveals a PHP code address.
